questions.q: Which command displays the LAST 10 lines of /var/log/syslog by default?
questions.note: tail prints the last 10 lines of a file by default. head prints the first 10 lines. cat prints the entire file. less opens a full interactive pager.

explain.correct: tail without flags prints the last 10 lines of the specified file by default.
wrong: head prints the FIRST 10 lines, not the last.
cat outputs the entire file, not just the final 10 lines.
less opens an interactive pager that displays the file from the beginning, not just the last 10 lines.

questions.q: You need to change only the group of /etc/report.conf to 'devops' without changing the owner. Which command is correct?
questions.note: chown :groupname changes only the group of a file when the user portion before the colon is omitted. chown username (no colon) changes only the owner, not the group.

explain.correct: chown :devops omits the user portion, so only the group is changed to 'devops'.
wrong: chmod changes permission bits, not the group or owner.
chown devops (no colon) changes the OWNER to 'devops', not the group.
setfacl adds an ACL entry for the group but does not change the file's primary group ownership.

questions.q: Which command recursively copies the directory /opt/app and all its contents to /backup/app?
questions.note: cp -r (or --recursive) copies a directory and all its subdirectories and files to the destination. Without -r, cp refuses to copy a directory. mv moves rather than copies.

explain.correct: cp -r copies the entire directory tree recursively to the destination.
wrong: mv moves the directory instead of copying it; the original is removed.
cp without -r will not copy a directory; it exits with an error.
tar is an archive tool, not a direct local recursive copy command.

questions.q: Which command creates both /home/alice and the nested subdirectory /home/alice/projects in one step?
questions.note: mkdir -p creates the full directory path, making parent directories as needed. Without -p, mkdir fails if a parent does not already exist. touch creates files, not directories.

explain.correct: mkdir -p creates all missing parent directories in the path without error.
wrong: touch -p is not valid; touch creates files and has no -p flag.
mkdir without -p fails if /home/alice does not already exist.
cp -r copies existing content; it does not create a new directory path.

questions.q: A script needs a lock file at /var/run/myjob.lock before running. Which single command creates that empty file?
questions.note: touch is the idiomatic command to create an empty file or update an existing file's timestamps. Copying from /dev/null also produces an empty file but touch is the standard tool for this purpose.

explain.correct: touch creates an empty file at the specified path if it does not exist.
wrong: mkdir creates a directory, not a file; this would create a directory named myjob.lock.
cp /dev/null works but is non-idiomatic; touch is the standard command for creating an empty file.
echo without a redirect prints text to stdout; it does not create a file at the given path.

questions.q: At the SUSE Linux boot menu, which option starts the system that is ALREADY installed on the hard drive rather than launching the installer?
questions.note: Boot from Hard Disk tells the bootloader to hand control to the installed OS on disk. All 'Installation' variants launch the installer. 'Rescue System' boots a minimal recovery environment.

explain.correct: 'Boot from Hard Disk' loads the already-installed operating system from the local disk.
wrong: 'Installation' launches the OS installer from the install medium.
'Installation - Safe Settings' is still the installer, just with conservative hardware settings.
'Rescue System' boots a minimal recovery environment, not the installed OS.

questions.q: Which command brings the network interface enp0s3 DOWN (disables it)?
questions.note: ip link set <iface> down deactivates the interface so it stops sending and receiving packets. The keyword is 'down'; 'disable' and 'stop' are not valid ip link state words.

explain.correct: ip link set enp0s3 down deactivates the specified network interface.
wrong: ip link set enp0s3 up ACTIVATES the interface, the opposite of what is asked.
'disable' is not a valid ip link state; the correct keyword is 'down'.
'stop' is not a valid ip link state; the correct keyword is 'down'.

questions.q: You run ping 8.8.8.8 and it keeps sending packets indefinitely. What keyboard shortcut stops it and prints the summary?
questions.note: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the foreground process, causing ping to stop and print its packet statistics. Ctrl-Z suspends (pauses) the process without printing stats. Ctrl-D signals end-of-input.

explain.correct: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to ping, stopping it and printing the statistics summary.
wrong: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, which suspends (backgrounds) the process without terminating it.
Ctrl-D signals end-of-input on stdin; it does not interrupt a running ping.
Ctrl-X is a text-editor binding (e.g., nano); it does not interrupt a process in the shell.

questions.q: Which ping flag limits the number of ECHO REQUEST packets sent to exactly 5?
questions.note: ping -c count sends exactly that many packets then exits. -w sets a deadline in seconds regardless of packets sent. -t sets the IP TTL (on some systems). -n suppresses DNS lookups and takes no count argument.

explain.correct: ping -c 5 sends exactly 5 ECHO REQUEST packets then exits.
wrong: -w 5 sets a 5-second deadline; ping exits after 5 seconds regardless of how many packets were sent.
-t sets the IP Time To Live field, not a packet count.
-n outputs numeric addresses only and does not take a packet count.

questions.q: Which DNS record type maps a hostname directly to an IPv4 address?
questions.note: An A record maps a hostname to a 32-bit IPv4 address. An AAAA record does the same for IPv6. MX routes mail. CNAME is an alias. PTR maps an IP back to a hostname (reverse lookup).

explain.correct: An A (Address) record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.
wrong: MX (Mail Exchanger) records designate the mail server for a domain, not a hostname-to-IP mapping.
CNAME is a canonical name alias pointing to another hostname, not directly to an IP.
PTR is a pointer record used for reverse DNS lookups (IP to hostname).

questions.q: Which octal permission digit activates the sticky bit on a directory when added to the three standard permission octets?
questions.note: In the four-digit octal permission notation, the sticky bit is represented by 1 in the leading digit (e.g., chmod 1777 /tmp). 4 is SUID, 2 is SGID, and 6 combines SUID+SGID.

explain.correct: The sticky bit is represented by octal 1 in the special-permission digit (e.g., 1777).
wrong: Octal 4 in the special digit sets the SUID bit, not the sticky bit.
Octal 2 in the special digit sets the SGID bit, not the sticky bit.
Octal 6 combines SUID (4) and SGID (2); it does not set the sticky bit.

questions.q: Which type of ACL includes named-user and named-group entries BEYOND the standard owner, owning-group, and other entries?
questions.note: An extended ACL adds named-user (user:name:perms) and named-group (group:name:perms) entries plus a mask entry on top of the three standard entries that form a minimum ACL.

explain.correct: An extended ACL adds named-user and named-group entries beyond the standard three, requiring a mask entry.
wrong: A minimum ACL contains ONLY the three standard entries matching conventional permission bits.
'basic' is informal and typically synonymous with minimum ACL; it does not include named entries.
A default ACL is inherited by new files in a directory; it describes when ACL entries apply, not which type adds named entries.

questions.q: Which command creates a compressed tar archive named backup.tar.gz from the /home/user directory?
questions.note: tar -czf creates (-c) a gzip-compressed (-z) archive written to the named file (-f). The -x flag extracts rather than creates. zip uses a different archive format. gzip compresses single files, not directory trees.

explain.correct: tar -czf backup.tar.gz /home/user creates a gzip-compressed tar archive of the directory.
wrong: tar -xzf EXTRACTS an existing archive; it does not create one.
zip produces a .zip archive, a different format from .tar.gz.
gzip operates on individual files; running it on a directory without tar does not produce a multi-file archive.

questions.q: In a Bash script, which syntax correctly computes 7 multiplied by 3 and stores the result in variable 'result'?
questions.note: The $(( )) arithmetic expansion evaluates integer expressions and is the POSIX-standard way to perform arithmetic in Bash. let also works but uses = not ==. Spaces around = in assignment are a syntax error.

explain.correct: result=$((7 * 3)) uses Bash arithmetic expansion to evaluate the expression and assign the result.
wrong: result = 7 * 3 has spaces around = which makes the shell interpret 'result' as a command, not an assignment.
result=$(7 * 3) runs 7 as a command in a subshell; it does not perform arithmetic expansion.
let result == 7 * 3 uses == (comparison) instead of = (assignment), so the variable is never set correctly.

questions.q: In a Makefile, what comes immediately after the target name on the dependency line, separated by a colon?
questions.note: A Makefile rule is structured as 'target: prerequisites' on the dependency line, followed by indented commands on subsequent lines. The prerequisites (dependencies) list what must exist or be built first.

explain.correct: After the colon on a Makefile rule's first line come the prerequisites — files or targets that must be built before the target.
wrong: Build commands appear on the indented lines below the target: prerequisites line, not on the same line after the colon.
Compiler flags appear inside the command lines or in variable definitions, not directly after the colon on the dependency line.
The output file name IS the target (before the colon), not what follows the colon.

questions.q: Which command-line tool captures and displays live network packets on a Linux interface for traffic analysis?
questions.note: tcpdump captures network packets on a specified interface and displays or saves them for analysis. df reports filesystem disk usage, free reports memory, and lsblk lists block devices.

explain.correct: tcpdump captures and displays live network traffic on a specified interface.
wrong: df reports disk filesystem usage; it is not a network traffic tool.
free reports RAM and swap usage; it is not a network traffic tool.
lsblk lists block storage devices; it is not a network traffic tool.

questions.q: On a SysV init system using chkconfig, which command ensures the 'sshd' service starts automatically at runlevels 3 and 5?
questions.note: chkconfig <service> on enables the service at its default runlevels (typically 2, 3, 4, and 5). 'enable', 'start', and the --level form with 'start' are not valid chkconfig syntax.

explain.correct: chkconfig sshd on enables the service to start automatically at the service's default runlevels.
wrong: 'enable' is not a valid chkconfig action; the correct keyword is 'on'.
'start' is not a chkconfig action for enabling at boot; it is an init script action.
chkconfig --level uses 'on' or 'off', not 'start', to control runlevel activation.

questions.q: On a SysV init system, which command starts the 'mysqld' service using its init script?
questions.note: The 'service' command invokes the appropriate init script to control a running service. chkconfig manages runlevel enablement. sysctl sets kernel parameters. 'rcmysqld enable' is not a valid init-script action.

explain.correct: service mysqld start invokes /etc/init.d/mysqld start to start the running service.
wrong: chkconfig manages whether a service is enabled at boot runlevels; it does not start or stop a running instance.
sysctl reads and sets kernel parameters; it has no service management function.
The rc<service> scripts accept 'start'/'stop'/'status', not 'enable'; and 'enable' is a systemctl concept.

questions.q: Which field in an /etc/fstab entry specifies the order in which fsck checks filesystems at boot?
questions.note: The sixth field in /etc/fstab (fs_passno) controls fsck check order at boot. 0 = skip, 1 = root filesystem (checked first), 2 = other filesystems checked in parallel. Field 5 (fs_freq) controls dump frequency.

explain.correct: Field 6 (fs_passno) sets the fsck pass number — 0 skips, 1 is the root FS, 2 means check after root.
wrong: Field 3 (fs_type) specifies the filesystem type (e.g., ext4, swap, xfs), not the fsck order.
Field 4 (fs_mntops) specifies mount options (e.g., defaults, noatime), not the fsck order.
Field 5 (fs_freq) controls how often dump backs up the filesystem (0 = never), not fsck order.

questions.q: Which command activates all swap partitions and files listed in /etc/fstab?
questions.note: swapon -a enables all swap spaces listed in /etc/fstab. mkswap initializes a swap area on a partition but does not activate it. swapoff -a disables all swap. mount -a mounts filesystems, not swap.

explain.correct: swapon -a activates all swap partitions and files defined in /etc/fstab.
wrong: mount -a mounts all filesystems in /etc/fstab; it does not activate swap partitions.
mkswap initializes (formats) a device or file as swap space but does not activate it.
swapoff -a DEACTIVATES all swap spaces, the opposite of enabling them.

questions.q: Which command displays the number of currently running processes, memory usage, and per-process CPU in a live, auto-refreshing view?
questions.note: top provides a live, auto-refreshing view of CPU usage, memory, load average, and per-process stats. ps aux gives a static snapshot. vmstat reports memory and I/O stats. df -h shows disk usage.

explain.correct: top displays a continuously updated, interactive view of process activity and system resource usage.
wrong: ps aux outputs a static, one-time snapshot of all processes; it does not auto-refresh.
vmstat reports virtual memory, I/O, and CPU statistics but does not show per-process detail.
df -h reports filesystem disk space usage, not process or CPU information.

questions.q: In a Bash script, the very first line is '#!/bin/bash'. The #! is called the shebang. What does the # character do on ALL other lines?
options: It marks the start of a block comment spanning multiple lines.
It begins a single-line comment; the shell ignores everything after it on that line.
It is an escape character that prevents the next character from being interpreted.
It signals the shell to run the rest of the line as a subshell.
questions.note: In shell scripts, # starts a comment that extends to the end of the line. Bash has no block comment syntax; multi-line comments require # on each line. The shebang (#! on line 1) is the only special case.

explain.correct: On any line other than the shebang, # begins a comment; the shell ignores everything from # to the end of the line.
wrong: Bash has no block comment syntax. # only comments out the rest of a single line; you must prefix every line individually.
The backslash \ is Bash's escape character, not #.
A subshell is invoked with $( ) or parentheses; # has no such effect.

questions.q: Which rsync flag preserves symbolic links, permissions, timestamps, and group/owner information during a remote transfer?
questions.note: rsync -a (archive mode) is equivalent to -rlptgoD: it preserves symlinks, permissions, timestamps, group, owner, and device files while also copying recursively. -r is recursive only. -z enables compression. -n is a dry run.

explain.correct: rsync -a (archive mode) recursively copies and preserves symlinks, permissions, timestamps, group, and owner.
wrong: -r copies recursively but does NOT preserve permissions, timestamps, symlinks, or ownership.
-z enables gzip compression of data in transit; it does not preserve metadata.
-n performs a dry run (no files are actually transferred).

questions.q: Which file would you edit to change the primary DNS nameserver that a Linux host uses for name resolution?
questions.note: /etc/resolv.conf lists the nameserver IP addresses (and optional search domains) used by the system resolver. /etc/hosts provides static name-to-IP mappings. /etc/hostname sets the machine's own name. nsswitch.conf controls the resolution order.

explain.correct: /etc/resolv.conf specifies the DNS nameserver addresses used for name resolution.
wrong: /etc/hostname stores the machine's own hostname, not its DNS server configuration.
/etc/hosts provides static local hostname-to-IP mappings but does not define which DNS server to query.
/etc/nsswitch.conf controls the ORDER in which resolution methods (files, dns, mdns) are tried, but the nameserver IPs are in /etc/resolv.conf.

questions.q: Which command displays the current Access Control List entries for the file /srv/data/report.csv?
questions.note: getfacl reads and prints the ACL entries of a file or directory. setfacl MODIFIES ACL entries. lsacl and chacl are not standard commands on most Linux distributions.

explain.correct: getfacl displays all ACL entries (owner, group, named users/groups, mask, other) for the specified file.
wrong: setfacl SETS or MODIFIES ACL entries; it does not display them.
lsacl is not a standard Linux command for viewing ACLs.
chacl is not a standard command on mainstream Linux distributions; it is specific to IRIX/SGI systems.
